author: Philip K. Dick
date_display: The Magazine of Fantasy & Science Fiction, 1953
card_summary: An unnamed man crushes two eavesdropping caterpillars under his foot on his way to the bus, cautiously avoids a spider web, and rides home uneasy about an insect world he half-perceives is aware of him.
page_summary:
An unnamed man crushes two eavesdropping caterpillars under his foot on his way to the bus, cautiously avoids a spider web, and rides home uneasy about an insect world he half-perceives is aware of him. Interleaved with his day are scenes among a society of insects — ants worshipped by their kind as gods, deliberating in council whether to move against 'the giant' who has somehow learned of their existence and organization. That night he walks into a spider's warning — 'wait... careful... inside' — ignores it, and finds his house's carpet has become a flood of attacking ants, which he beats back with a garden hose. Three spiders then visit him at his desk: a Cruncher, a Spinner, and a Stinger, who explain the deep history he has stumbled into. A billion years ago, humans came from another planet to a world already cultivated by the ants' ancestors; a war between the two reduced both sides, and the surviving humans who knew the truth bred spiders — 'the Eaters' — to keep the ant civilization in permanent check. As the sound of the ants' full mobilization rises beneath the floorboards, the man asks the spiders if they can save him. They are embarrassed: they meant the species, not him personally.

**Why it matters.** At under two thousand words the story does almost nothing except set up its final joke, but the joke is exact: the man has spent the whole story being an individual in fear for his individual life, and the story's closing correction — 'I meant the species... not you as an individual' — refuses him even the dignity of being the protagonist of his own crisis. The ant civilization's parliamentary cruelty (debating whether the man is worth the trouble of destroying) and the spiders' genuinely ancient, disinterested loyalty to the human species rather than to any human give the story a coldness unusual even by the standard of Dick's other 1950s insect and paranoia stories.

*The man's last line — 'I see... I'm sorry I misunderstood you' — is the story's only moment of real dignity: not fear, but an apology for a category error he never had the information to avoid.*

structure.form: short story in three brief movements, cold and comic by turns
movements: The morning: the caterpillars killed, the spider web avoided, a day's uneasy peace.
Cut to the ant council debating whether to move against him at all — he is judged not dangerous enough to bother killing quickly.
The night attack, the spiders' explanation of the ancient war, and the closing correction of scale.
structure.point_of_view: alternates between the man and the insect councils without transition, so the reader is given privileged access neither side has to the other — a structural joke that pays off in the final line.
structure.central_device: A punchline built entirely on a category error: the man asks to be personally saved and is told, apologetically, that the promise was only ever for his species.

characters.name: The man
characters.note: Ordinary and quietly paranoid from the first paragraph — he already suspects birds and spiders of being 'in on it' before anything has actually happened to him.

characters.name: Tirmus
characters.note: Argues for restraint on grounds of economy of force, not mercy — 'someday we'll need it' — and loses the vote.

characters.name: Lala
characters.note: Insists the man's mere knowledge of the ants' existence is intolerable, regardless of his inability to act on it.

characters.name: The Cruncher, the Spinner, the Stinger
characters.note: Chatty and matter-of-fact about a war a billion years old and a mission that has nothing to do with any individual human's survival.

settings.name: The suburban street and house
settings.note: Cherry tree, mailbox, bus stop, garden hose — an entirely ordinary domestic setting revealed to be a battlefield in a war older than the species.

settings.name: The ant council's mound
settings.note: A deliberative body with recognizable statecraft — votes, factions, strategic patience — mapped directly onto insects.

motifs: Insects as a fully realized political and religious society, with their own gods, wars, and statesmen, running parallel to and unnoticed by human life
Warnings given and ignored, exactly at the moment they would have mattered
Scale as the story's punchline: a war spanning a billion years and an entire species, delivered to a man worried only about himself
Cold competence in both insect societies — neither the ants' cruelty nor the spiders' loyalty is sentimental

distinctive_terms.label: Gods
distinctive_terms.note: The ants are addressed and address each other as gods without irony within their own council scenes.

distinctive_terms.label: March
distinctive_terms.note: The ant army's mobilization, framed in explicitly military language.

pkd_on_this_work.summary: Dick's own letters record confusion about the retitling of the story from his original title.

evidence.quote: I am pleased-surprised>thankful. But I am puzzled by the new title "Expendable." What does it mean? How does it fit the story? Who put it on? And — is there any way I can get hold
evidence.reading: Dick genuinely did not choose or immediately understand the published title, which retrospectively fits the story's punchline about being expendable as an individual precisely.

evidence.quote: "Expendable." 1953 Fantasy House. First appeared in The Magazine of Fantasy & Science-Fiction.
evidence.reading: Bibliographic confirmation of the original title change from 'Left Shoe, My Foot' and the sale details.

evidence.author: Christopher Palmer
evidence.quote: dogs: "Roog" (1953, CS1) and "Adjustment Team" (1954, CS2); spiders: "Expendable" (1953, CS1)
evidence.reading: Palmer catalogs this among Dick's recurring animal-perception devices — non-human creatures granted awareness humans lack.

evidence.author: Anne R. Dick
evidence.quote: everything in that world is out to 'get' the colonists, from pseudo-microscopes to pseudo-spaceships. In "Expendable," the bugs are out to get everybody (except for the spiders). Eventually, the spiders will win, but
evidence.reading: Anne Dick, Dick's second wife, situating the story within a broader pattern of persecutory, adversarial worlds across his fiction — a first-person account of the recurring paranoid structure rather than a formal analysis.

open_questions: Dick's letter asking who chose the title 'Expendable' is cut off before any reply is captured — was the question ever answered in a later letter?
Anne Dick's sentence about the spiders eventually winning is cut off; the fuller passage might connect this story more explicitly to others she discusses nearby.
The original title 'Left Shoe, My Foot' has no evident connection to the story as published — worth checking whether an earlier draft or synopsis explains it.

reading_provenance.note: Close reading of the primary text plus attributed evidence from the archive. Candidate: not yet promoted to canonical.
